newsitem.title: USA: South Dakota cattle death toll continues to rise.
newsitem.headline: South Dakota cattle death toll continues to rise.

text.p: The death toll in South Dakota cattle is rising after possibly the worst winter storms this century, government and industry sources said Monday.
Storm-related deaths could continue for months as cows, some of which went without feed for two weeks, have either stillborn calves or offspring which die shortly after birth.

"We are continuing to see death loss of animals that were stressed earlier and we are anticipating real problems with our calving season," said Tim Alcorn, public information officer for South Dakota's Department of Agriculture.
Alcorn said the northern third of the state was the worst affected. He estimated there were 1.8 to 1.9 million head of cattle in that area, out of the state's total of 3.9 million.
He declined to estimate the death toll to date.
"There are so many (cattle) that we are not able to find yet it is hard to be accurate," Alcorn said.
Tonya Ness, executive secretary of the South Dakota Cattlemen's Association, said she had heard talk that some herds in the north had losses of up to 75 percent.
She said two percent of her cows in central South Dakota had died and a higher percentage of calves may be lost.
"We will continue to see effects from this into October," she said.
State veterinarian Sam Holland said it might be the worst winter for livestock deaths since the late 19th century.

He noted most of the cattle in South Dakota were for breeding. There were reports that some cows had frozen udders and would be unable to feed their young, while some bulls suffered damage to testicles during the storms, he said.
Holland said the largest death loss was within three to four days of a storm but subsequent calving and other losses over the next few months would be "significant".
A spokeswoman for the government's Farm Service Agency in Huron, South Dakota said the death toll as of January 17 was 35,000 head and the USDA was in the process of updating that total.
Alcorn, of South Dakota's Department of Agriculture, noted that temperatures were slightly warmer on Monday, helping to slow the death toll.
"It (the death rate) has to an extent slowed. We are having snow today but it is warmer. We are not having the bone chilling cold we have had to deal with before," he said.

USDA announced Friday a new cost-share assistance program to help producers provide feed for storm-stricken livestock in the Dakotas and 35 contiguous counties following a tour of the region by Deputy Agriculture Secretary Richard Rominger.
